prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which many neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength are interrogated at optical frequencies, bringing clock uncertainties to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single part for B040, Hidetoshi Katori and Jun Ye. The first round did not rest on counting heads, since seven members reach the same pair from different fields and for different reasons, but it did sharpen what the case is. The scientific content is one physical idea and its development: a lattice at the magic wavelength makes the trap-induced shift of the clock transition vanish to first order, so thousands of neutral atoms can be interrogated together with long coherence. That is what let optical clocks combine the statistical power of an ensemble with the systematic control once reserved for a single ion. The consequence is demonstrated, not promised: fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 reproduced and compared across independent laboratories, and the clocks already used for tests of fundamental constants and for height differences through gravitational redshift. The chair asked for one sentence on what the clock adds beyond 2005 and 2012. My answer is that the 2005 prize honoured the comb as a ruler for counting optical frequencies and the 2012 prize honoured control of one quantum system at a time, while the lattice clock solves a different problem, how to probe a large neutral ensemble without a light-shift penalty. I would put that sentence into the citation itself, species-neutral, so the prize is for the principle and its development and not for one element or one record.
statement.case_against: The distinctness objection is still the real one and I do not think the committee should pretend otherwise. Ye shared the 2005 prize, and Danielsson is right that comb-based spectroscopy is part of the technical lineage in which his lattice-clock work was done; the 2012 prize also covered the ion route to precision. A reader could still describe this as a third award in one measurement tradition. I judge the physical idea to be separable, but that is a judgement and not a proof. Two further weaknesses remain. Lemonde, Hollberg, Ludlow, Takamoto and the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups sit outside a two-name credit, and the supplied material does not settle Katori's concept against Ye's accuracy work beyond the two roles. Also, the redefinition of the second has not happened, so I will not allow it into the citation.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers B018 (Halzen and Karle) as a new observational channel, regards the lattice clock as a third step in one measurement lineage after 2005 and 2012, and asks whether my not ranking B018 reflects doubt about attribution or about maturity.
responses.response: Both, and neither amounts to a doubt about the importance of the detection. On attribution, a two-name credit for a collaboration of hundreds, with AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND outside it and with you saying you have not verified who was decisive for the first events, is harder for me to defend than the clock credit. On maturity, I am an atomic physicist and cannot judge source astronomy at your level, but by your own account the origin of the bulk of the diffuse flux is unsettled and independent confirmation is still developing, whereas the clock is already reproduced at the claimed level by several laboratories. On continuity, I concede that the comb and the ion clock are real predecessors and I count that as the main weakness of B040. I still think the lattice is a different principle: it is not a better ruler or a better single particle, it is a way to use many atoms at once without shifting the line. You list B040 as your first alternative and say you would not object strongly, which I take seriously. I would ask you to say whether a citation that states the lattice idea in its own words meets your distinctness test.

responses.point: Lindroth asks that the citation state the new element, a neutral-atom ensemble at a magic wavelength interrogated at optical frequency, and asks whether independent 1e-18 comparisons are enough without the redefinition of the second.
responses.response: I agree and have changed my draft accordingly: the citation above now says what the lattice does instead of only naming the clock. On maturity I would answer yes to your last question. The criterion is a demonstrated invention, and agreement between independent clocks at the 1e-18 level is demonstrated whichever way the standards bodies decide about the second. I also keep your point that Katori's idea and Ye's accuracy record are the two threads later strontium and ytterbium clocks follow, and I still would not rank the two names against each other.

responses.point: Olsson would divide the citation by roles and press whether the first strontium realisation should be named so that Lemonde and others cannot claim a priority objection, while judging the work on first operation and its uncertainty budget.
responses.response: I take the priority concern, but I come out the other way on naming strontium. The lattice clock has been realised with both strontium and ytterbium, and a citation naming one element would invite a dispute that the evidence does not need. A species-neutral wording that states the magic-wavelength condition covers the invention, and the word development covers Ye's contribution to accuracy and stability. I accept your test of first operation and uncertainty budget as the way to settle roles if the record ever demands it, but the supplied material does not allow a finer split, so I would not write one into the citation.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, asks whether the committee accepts the lattice clock as distinct, whether to use a two-name credit with the wider community recorded, and how to handle the Kroll disclosure.
responses.response: On distinctness I would accept the one-sentence statement above as the committee's formulation. On credit, I would keep the pair and record Lemonde, Hollberg, Ludlow and the institutional groups in the committee's own notes as contributors, since I have seen no evidence in the shortlist for a third name that is stronger than the two-name credit. On my own disclosure, my research stay in Hall's laboratory was a doctoral-period visit, and I have no tie to Katori or Ye. I think the committee can reasonably decide that it does not require recusal, but I will abide by its decision.

responses.point: Mehlig prefers a citation worded around the invention and development and not around record figures, and regards QKD (B010) as protocol-level with heavier overlap with the 2022 prize than I allowed.
responses.response: I accept the first point and have kept record numbers out of the preferred wording beyond naming the 10^-18 level as the scale of the achievement. On B010, I take your overlap argument and it lowers my confidence in it, so I keep it only as an alternative and would not argue for a second part built around it. A single part is my preference for the same reason you give for B040: it is the configuration whose scientific statement the committee can make in one sentence.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize, which is a judgement and not something the evidence settles.
Whether Danielsson would join a B040 prize, and whether the committee should treat B018 as a serious alternative for a later year.
How to record Lemonde, Hollberg, Ludlow, Takamoto and the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups when the credit is limited to two names; I have no evidence for a third name.
Whether a second part, B010 or B061, would add anything the committee can defend on attribution and overlap; I currently see none.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure: my doctoral period included a research stay in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, and Hall shares the 2005 prize that bounds B040. I have no documented tie to Katori or Ye, and I disclose the Hall connection so that the committee can decide whether recusal is warranted; I do not think it is, but I will accept its decision. I am also an experimental atomic physicist working on laser spectroscopy and optical quantum memories at Lund, close to the field of B040 but not in clock work, which I mention for completeness.
